notes.b: Weathering is the breakdown of rock in place at or near the earth's surface, by weather, water, plants and animals. Erosion is the wearing away and removal of material by a moving agent such as a river, the sea, ice or wind.
points: Weathering involves no transport: the rock breaks down where it lies, and this prepares it for erosion and mass movement.
Regolith is the layer of loose, weathered rock fragments lying on top of solid bedrock.
Physical (mechanical) weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its minerals.
Chemical weathering changes or dissolves the minerals in the rock.
Biological weathering by plants and animals works through both physical and chemical means.

notes.b: Freeze-thaw action, also called frost shattering, needs temperatures that move above and below 0 °C often, together with water and jointed rock.
points: Water enters cracks and joints in the rock.
At night the water freezes and expands by about 9%, widening the crack.
By day the ice thaws, and the water seeps deeper into the crack.
Repeated cycles of freezing and thawing split off angular fragments.
It is most effective on mountains in upland Ireland, on high mountains and in periglacial areas; freeze-thaw is active on Irish mountain summits such as Carrauntoohil, Co. Kerry.
Result: scree (talus) slopes of angular fragments at the foot of mountain cliffs, and jagged peaks and blockfields.
Exfoliation, or onion weathering, is an insolation process in hot deserts such as the Sahara, where the daily temperature range is large.
The outer layer of rock heats and expands by day, and cools and contracts at night more than the interior, because rock conducts heat poorly.
Stress builds up, and curved outer sheets peel off like the layers of an onion, leaving rounded boulders.
Many geographers stress that some moisture, such as dew, must be present for exfoliation to work effectively.
Granular disintegration: dark and light minerals in a rock such as granite heat and expand at different rates, so individual grains loosen and fall away, leaving gravelly sand.
Pressure release (sheeting): when the overlying rock is eroded, buried rock such as granite expands upward and cracks into sheets parallel to the surface.
The sheets peel off to leave domes, such as Half Dome, Yosemite, California, USA.
Salt crystallisation: salt water enters pores and cracks; as it evaporates, salt crystals grow and force the rock apart.
Salt crystallisation is common in hot deserts and on coasts.
Plant roots grow into cracks and widen them, and burrowing animals expose fresh rock to weathering.
Decaying plants produce humic acids, and lichens and mosses release acids that attack rock surfaces.

notes.b: Carbonation dissolves limestone, and it works along joints and bedding planes.
points: Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil to form weak carbonic acid.
The acid reacts with calcium carbonate in limestone to form calcium bicarbonate, which is soluble and is carried away in solution.
Word equation: calcium carbonate + water + carbon dioxide gives calcium bicarbonate.
Carbonation is the process behind karst; it operates on the Carboniferous limestone of the Burren, Co. Clare.
Hydrolysis: water reacts with feldspar in granite and turns it into clay (kaolin, or china clay); the quartz grains are left as sand, and the granite crumbles.
China clay from the hydrolysis of granite is quarried around St Austell, Cornwall, England, and on the edge of Dartmoor.
Oxidation: oxygen dissolved in water reacts with iron in the rock to form iron oxide (rust), which gives red, yellow or brown colours and weakens the rock.
Hydration: some minerals absorb water and swell, setting up stress; anhydrite, for example, becomes gypsum.
Solution: some minerals, such as rock salt, dissolve directly in water.

notes.h: Factors influencing weathering: climate and rock
points: Climate: temperature and rainfall decide which type of weathering dominates.
Warm, wet climates favour fast chemical weathering; by Van 't Hoff's rule, the rate of chemical reactions roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature.
Cold climates with temperatures around freezing favour freeze-thaw, and hot deserts favour exfoliation and salt crystallisation.
Ireland's mild, wet climate favours chemical weathering.
Rock type: limestone is vulnerable to carbonation, granite to hydrolysis, and quartzite resists both.

notes.h: Factors influencing weathering: structure, cover, time and relief
points: Rock structure: joints, bedding planes and faults let water in, so heavily jointed rock weathers faster.
Vegetation and soil: roots and humic acids speed weathering, and soil holds moisture against the rock.
Time: older surfaces are more weathered.
Relief and aspect: steep slopes remove debris and expose fresh rock, and shady slopes stay frozen longer, so freeze-thaw is stronger on them.
Temperature acts in two ways: as a trigger, through the expansion and contraction that cause stress, and as a control on the rate of chemical reactions.
Freeze-thaw depends on temperature crossing the freezing point, and exfoliation and granular disintegration depend on a large daily range; both need changes in temperature, not just warmth.
Warmth speeds the chemical reactions of carbonation and hydrolysis, so the same temperature can favour chemical weathering in one place and freeze-thaw in another.
Method: name the process and its type, state the temperature condition it needs, explain the stress or rate change it produces, and link this to the result, such as scree from freeze-thaw.

factCards.definition: Physical: plant roots grow into cracks and widen them; burrowing animals expose fresh rock. Chemical: decaying plants produce humic acids; lichens and mosses release acids that attack rock surfaces.

factCards.term: Climate: which type of weathering each climate favours
factCards.definition: Warm, wet: fast chemical weathering, as reaction rates roughly double for every 10 °C rise (Van 't Hoff's rule). Cold, around freezing: freeze-thaw. Hot deserts: exfoliation and salt crystallisation. Ireland's mild, wet climate favours chemical weathering.

factCards.term: Role of temperature in physical weathering: the three processes and why
factCards.definition: Freeze-thaw needs temperatures crossing the freezing point; exfoliation and granular disintegration need a large daily range, as rock and its minerals expand and contract unevenly. In each, temperature change, not just warmth, causes the stress.

questions.prompt: Explain the role of temperature in the process of physical (mechanical) weathering.
questions.model: Temperature is the driving factor in physical weathering, acting through expansion and contraction. Freeze-thaw action is the main example. Temperatures must move above and below 0 °C often, with water and jointed rock present. Water enters cracks, freezes at night and expands by about 9%, widening the crack; it thaws by day and seeps deeper. Repeated cycles split off angular fragments, which collect as scree slopes at the foot of mountain cliffs, and produce jagged peaks and blockfields. This is most effective on mountains in upland Ireland, on high mountains and in periglacial areas. Exfoliation, or onion weathering, depends on a large daily temperature range in hot deserts such as the Sahara. The outer layer of rock heats and expands by day and cools and contracts at night more than the interior, because rock conducts heat poorly. Stress builds up and curved outer sheets peel off, leaving rounded boulders; some moisture such as dew helps the process. Granular disintegration depends on temperature too: dark and light minerals in granite expand at different rates, so the grains loosen and fall away as gravelly sand. In each case the temperature change, not the temperature alone, produces the stress. By contrast, chemical weathering is controlled by temperature as a rate: reactions roughly double for every 10 °C rise, so it is fastest in warm, wet climates.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain any two of the following types of weathering: freeze-thaw action, carbonation, onion weathering.
questions.model: Freeze-thaw action is a physical process. It needs temperatures that move above and below 0 °C often, with water and jointed rock. Water enters cracks and joints; it freezes at night and expands by about 9%, widening the crack. By day it thaws and seeps deeper. Repeated cycles split off angular fragments, which build up as scree at the foot of mountain cliffs. It is most effective on mountains in upland Ireland and high mountains. Carbonation is a chemical process. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil to form weak carbonic acid. The acid reacts with calcium carbonate in limestone to form calcium bicarbonate, which is soluble and is carried away in solution. It works along joints and bedding planes, as on the Carboniferous limestone of the Burren, Co. Clare, and it is the process behind karst.

questions.prompt: Name two factors that influence weathering and explain one of them.
questions.model: Two factors are climate and rock type. Climate decides which type of weathering dominates: warm, wet climates favour fast chemical weathering, since reaction rates roughly double for every 10 °C rise in temperature, while cold climates with temperatures around freezing favour freeze-thaw. Rock type also matters, because limestone is vulnerable to carbonation and granite to hydrolysis.
